domain: Web app technical support (email delivery reliability)
schema_note: Mirrors INESCTEC_RESEARCH.md section 3/4 output schema exactly, same convention as conversations/rest_api/ground_truth.json. hierarchical labels: subcase|supercase|same_level. pragmatic labels: revises|contradicts|resolves|depends_on|references. state_node types: goal|decision|constraint|open_question. retrieval_count is set equal to recurrence_count throughout, per the worked example's own convention for a static, hand-built corpus (real runs diverge). Entity taxonomy extended for this domain with exactly one addition beyond the default set: 'feature' = a named product feature or UI element (e.g. the 'Resend email' button) that doesn't fit person/organization/system/location/document/tool/event/measurement/other. Deliberately built (per the Phase 3 plan, evaluation_report.md section 'Build the technical support corpus') to exercise labels the rest_api corpus structurally under-represents: contradicts (x2 here), supercase (x2, both the explicit-review pattern and the implicit-generalisation pattern), decision:reverted, decision:revised, goal:abandoned, constraint:lifted.

schema_findings.issue: Marking a goal 'abandoned' (SN_5) and a decision 'reverted' (SN_7, at N_13) has no corresponding StateRelation label - 'abandoned'/'reverted' are status values, not one of {supports, contradicts, constrained_by, resolves}.
schema_findings.proposed_direction: Used state_node_links.updates alone (direct status assignment) for these, with no paired relates entry, since forcing one of the four StateRelation labels onto a status change they don't describe would misrepresent the relation. relates is only populated when the touching interaction's relationship to the state node is itself one of the four labels (e.g. N_12 constrained_by SN_6, separately from the same turn's updates=[[SN_5,'abandoned']]).

schema_findings.issue: SN_7 (the timeout-increase decision) and SN_9 (background-queue-as-future-project goal) never receive a citation or explicit revisit after their creation turn besides the ones that change their status - unlike rest_api's SN_3 which accumulated several 'supports' touches over the conversation.
schema_findings.proposed_direction: Left as-is deliberately: not every state node needs ongoing engagement to be realistic, and forcing extra touches purely for annotation density would be the same over-connection risk flagged in evaluation_report.md's error analysis of predicted (not gold) graphs. A thin touch history on a minor, quickly-superseded decision is the realistic case, not a gap to fix.

N_1.question: We're seeing complaints that some users aren't getting their password reset emails. Looks like around 5% of reset requests never result in an email showing up. Where should we start looking?
N_1.answer: Start with the basics — check whether these emails are even being sent successfully on your end, or whether they're being sent but not delivered. If they're being sent fine, the most common cause at that failure rate is spam filtering on the receiving end. Do you have SPF and DKIM set up for your sending domain?
N_1.summary: Reports ~5% of password-reset emails never arrive; agent suspects spam filtering and asks about SPF/DKIM.

N_2.question: I don't think so, actually — we've never explicitly configured either. Could that really cause a 5% failure rate?
N_2.answer: Yes, easily. Without SPF and DKIM, a lot of mail providers will silently drop or spam-file your emails, especially from a domain with no sending history. I'd set both up — SPF to declare which servers can send on your domain's behalf, DKIM to sign your emails so receivers can verify they're genuinely from you.
N_2.summary: Decides to add SPF and DKIM records to fix the suspected spam-filtering cause.

N_3.question: Okay, we've added SPF and DKIM records for our domain. How will we know if this actually fixes it, versus there being something else going on too?
N_3.answer: Track the reset-email delivery failure rate over the next couple of weeks — if SPF/DKIM was the whole problem, it should drop close to zero. Worth flagging as something to actively check back on rather than assuming it's solved immediately.
N_3.summary: Opens the question of whether SPF/DKIM will fully fix the delivery failures.

N_4.question: Following up — it's been two weeks. The failure rate dropped a bit, but we're still seeing about 2% of reset emails never arriving. I reached out to a few affected users directly and asked them to check their spam folder too — it's not there either. It's like it was never sent at all.
N_4.answer: That's a different symptom than spam filtering, then — if it's not even landing in spam, it's likely not being accepted on your sending side in the first place, not a delivery/filtering issue on the receiving end. How are you actually sending these emails right now, technically speaking?
N_4.summary: Reports 2% of resets still missing entirely (not in spam either), disputing the spam-filtering diagnosis.

N_5.question: We're using MailBridge — the shared email-sending account that came with our hosting plan. Password reset emails get sent directly from our app through that account whenever someone requests one.
N_5.answer: Worth checking closely — shared accounts like that often have a sending-volume limit per minute or hour, and once you're over it, the extra emails often just get silently dropped rather than bounced with a visible error. Do you ever get a burst of reset requests close together — like after a promotional email that gets a lot of people logging back in?
N_5.summary: Reveals password-reset emails are sent via MailBridge, a shared hosting-provided account.

N_6.question: Actually, yes — we sent a re-engagement email campaign last month that caused a spike in password reset requests right afterward, since a lot of people had forgotten their passwords.
N_6.answer: That lines up. I'd bet MailBridge's shared account is quietly rate-limiting you during those bursts, and the emails past the limit just disappear instead of erroring out where you'd notice. The real fix is to stop using a shared bulk-sending account for user-facing transactional email like this, and switch to a dedicated transactional email service instead — something like SendClear, which is built for exactly this and doesn't share sending limits with other customers.
N_6.summary: Confirms a sending burst pattern; root cause identified as MailBridge rate-limiting - fix is to switch to SendClear.
N_6.reference: Root cause found: MailBridge rate-limiting; switch to SendClear

N_7.question: We've switched password reset emails over to SendClear. Delivery failures have dropped to basically zero over the last few days. Should we worry about this for other emails we send too, or was this specific to password reset?
N_7.answer: Not specific to password reset at all — for the same reason [N_6], any user-facing email your app sends on someone's behalf should go through a dedicated service like SendClear rather than a shared bulk account: shared accounts aren't built to guarantee individual message delivery, especially under bursty sending. I'd treat that as a general rule going forward, not just a one-time fix for this email.
N_7.summary: Confirms SendClear fixed delivery failures and generalises the fix into a rule for all user-facing email.
N_7.reference: General rule: all user-facing email via dedicated service

N_8.question: Switching gears — separately, we're getting reports that the 'Resend email' button on the reset-password page sometimes just spins forever, especially when a lot of people are using the site at once. Any idea what's going on there?
N_8.answer: Most likely the button's request is waiting synchronously for the email to actually finish sending before it responds to the browser, and under load that send can take a while. What's your current request timeout set to?
N_8.summary: Reports the Resend email button hanging under load; agent suspects synchronous send + asks about timeout.
N_8.reference: Resend button hanging under load reported

N_9.question: Whatever the framework default is — I don't think we've ever touched it.
N_9.answer: As a first pass, bump the timeout up so the request has more room to complete rather than failing early. That won't fix the underlying slowness, but it should stop the spinner from erroring out prematurely while we look at the real cause.
N_9.summary: Decides to increase the request timeout as a first-pass mitigation.

N_10.question: We increased the timeout. It's better, but during busy periods it's still slow — sometimes 10+ seconds before the button responds.
N_10.answer: Right, the timeout bump was always a band-aid — it gives slow requests more room to finish, it doesn't make them faster. The real fix is to stop making the button wait on the email send at all: hand the email off to a background job and respond to the browser immediately, instead of sending it inline during the request.
N_10.summary: Reports the timeout increase was insufficient; proposes background-queue email sending as the real fix.

N_11.question: That sounds like a bigger change — we'd need some kind of background job queue, right? We don't have one set up currently.
N_11.answer: Right, you'd need a queue and a worker process to send emails asynchronously instead of inline. It's a common pattern, but it is new infrastructure, not just a config change.
N_11.summary: Confirms the background-queue approach would require new infrastructure.
N_11.reference: Background queue confirmed as new infrastructure

N_12.question: Unfortunately we can't take that on right now — we're in the middle of migrating our whole app to a new hosting provider, and the team's policy during the migration is no new infrastructure until that's done, to avoid complicating the cutover.
N_12.answer: That's a reasonable constraint. In that case let's not go the background-queue route yet. A smaller fix that doesn't need new infrastructure: trim what happens inside the request itself — skip any non-essential logging or lookups on that code path — so the synchronous send is as fast as it can be without adding a queue.
N_12.summary: States the infra-migration freeze constraint; agent proposes trimming the synchronous path instead of a queue.
N_12.reference: Infra freeze constraint; smaller fix proposed

N_13.question: We trimmed the unnecessary work out of the resend-email code path. Response times are consistently fast now, even during busy periods — the timeout increase we did earlier isn't even needed anymore, we could probably set it back to default.
N_13.answer: Good — let's actually do that, revert the timeout back to its original value. It was only ever meant to cover for the slow synchronous send [N_10], and now that the real slowness is fixed, leaving an inflated timeout in place just hides future problems instead of surfacing them.
N_13.summary: Confirms the trim fix resolved the slowness; agrees to revert the now-unneeded timeout increase.
N_13.reference: Trim fix confirmed; timeout increase reverted

N_14.question: Separate issue — a few users are saying their password reset link looks broken or expired the moment they click it, even though they just requested it seconds earlier.
N_14.answer: That's usually either a link-expiration time set too short, or a bug in how the link is built. Is this happening on the password-reset email specifically, or have you seen it anywhere else?
N_14.summary: Reports password reset links appearing broken/expired immediately after being sent.

N_15.question: Just the password-reset email, as far as we've seen.
N_15.answer: Okay, assuming it's isolated to that one for now. Can you check the order of operations in your code — is the reset token generated and saved before the email template renders the link, or could the template be rendering before the token actually exists?
N_15.summary: Confirms (incorrectly, per N_17) that the broken-link bug is isolated to the password-reset email.
N_15.reference: Bug assumed isolated to password-reset email

N_16.question: Looked into it — you're right, there's a race condition. The email template renders the reset link using the token immediately, but the token doesn't actually get saved to the database until just after, so occasionally the link is built from a token that isn't valid yet if the user clicks fast.
N_16.answer: That's the bug. Fix is to reorder it — save the token first, then only render and send the email once the token is confirmed saved, not before.
N_16.summary: Identifies the race condition (token saved after link render) and decides to reorder token-save before render.
N_16.reference: Race-condition bug found; reorder fix decided

N_17.question: Fixed it for the password-reset email — reordered so the token saves first. But while testing, I noticed the email verification email has the exact same bug — same broken-link-immediately-after-sending symptom.
N_17.answer: That actually makes sense — I'd guess both emails share the same underlying 'generate token, render, send' helper function, so the bug was never really isolated to password-reset, we just hadn't seen it reported for verification yet. Apply the same reorder fix inside the shared helper, not just the password-reset-specific code, so both emails are covered. Worth checking if any other emails use that same helper too, while you're in there.
N_17.summary: Reveals the verification email has the same bug, disputing that it was isolated to password-reset.
N_17.reference: Bug found to also affect verification email

N_18.question: Good catch — yes, they do share a helper. Fixed it there instead, so both emails are covered now.
N_18.answer: That's a better fix than patching each email separately would have been.
N_18.summary: Confirms the reorder fix was applied to the shared helper, covering both email types.
N_18.reference: Shared-helper fix applied, covers both emails

N_19.question: On that note — should verification emails also go through SendClear instead of MailBridge, like we did for password reset?
N_19.answer: Yes, same reasoning as before [N_7] — any user-facing transactional email should go through the dedicated service, not the shared account, regardless of which email it is.
N_19.summary: Asks whether verification emails should also move to SendClear; agent confirms per the general rule.
N_19.reference: Verification email routed to SendClear too

N_20.question: Makes sense, we'll migrate verification emails over to SendClear as well.
N_20.answer: Sounds good — that should close out most of the reliability issues we've been chasing across these threads.
N_20.summary: Confirms verification emails will migrate to SendClear.

N_21.question: Stepping back — we've now fixed the delivery failures and the broken-link bug separately. Are those actually related, or just two unrelated things that happened to surface around the same time?
N_21.answer: They're related only loosely, in that both are about email reliability, but they're genuinely separate problems with separate causes — one was emails not arriving at all, due to rate-limiting on the sending side; the other was emails arriving with a broken link, due to a timing bug in how the link gets built. Fixing one wouldn't have touched the other.
N_21.summary: Compares the delivery-failure fix and the broken-link fix as parallel but unrelated issues.

N_22.question: Quick update — the hosting migration finally finished last week, so the 'no new infrastructure' restriction doesn't apply anymore.
N_22.answer: Good to know. That means the background-queue approach for sending emails is worth putting back on the table now that it's actually feasible — not just for the resend button, but potentially for other slow user-facing actions too, if there are any worth looking at.
N_22.summary: Reports the hosting migration is complete; agent reopens the background-queue idea as feasible again.
N_22.reference: Infra freeze lifted; background queue reopened

N_23.question: Has the delivery failure rate stayed near zero since we switched to SendClear back in September?
N_23.answer: Yes — it's been consistently under 0.1% since the switch, which is about what you'd expect as background noise like typos in email addresses or full inboxes, not a real systemic issue anymore. I'd consider that one resolved.
N_23.summary: Confirms the delivery failure rate has stayed near zero; the original goal is considered achieved.

N_24.question: Before I write up a short postmortem for the team, can you give me a summary of everything we fixed across these threads?
N_24.answer: Sure — three separate fixes. First, password-reset and verification emails were switched from the shared MailBridge account to the dedicated SendClear service [N_6], fixing silent delivery failures caused by rate-limiting during sending bursts, with the general rule going forward that user-facing email should always go through a dedicated service. Second, the 'Resend email' button's slowness under load was fixed at the root by trimming the synchronous request path [N_13] rather than adding new infrastructure, since the hosting migration was blocking new infra at the time; the earlier timeout increase was reverted once it was no longer needed, and the background-queue idea is back on the table now that the migration is done. Third, a shared token-generation race condition was causing broken reset and verification links immediately after sending, fixed by reordering token-save before email-render inside the shared helper function [N_16].
N_24.summary: Consolidated review of all three fixes, ahead of a postmortem write-up.
N_24.reference: All three fixes reviewed for postmortem

N_25.question: That's a great summary, thanks. Now that the background-queue idea is back on the table, should we scope it out as a proper project, or fold it into something else?
N_25.answer: I'd scope it as its own small project rather than folding it in — it touches more than just the resend button if you want to use it for other slow actions too, so it deserves its own design pass rather than being squeezed into unrelated work. Not blocking anything right now, so no rush.
N_25.summary: Decides to scope the background-queue idea as its own future project.
N_25.reference: Background queue scoped as future project

N_26.question: Sounds good, I'll get that queued up as a separate task for next quarter. Thanks for all the help working through this.
N_26.answer: Happy to help — feel free to reach out if the delivery failure rate creeps back up, or anything else comes up.
N_26.summary: Closing turn; user will queue the future project, thanks the agent.
